skills.why: The owning workflow; its Plan stage (§4–5 step 1) scoped this treatment
Arc of the scene as the implementation footnote to the message, and the rhythm: reveal, hold, push, hold for the mechanism, pull back
Visual treatment: depth layers, colour meaning, and term and label typography at video scale
Borrowed method of pacing reveals to spoken cues inside one continuous frame (windows are not cuts), and the caption-band keep-out
Directing one dominant motif (the token level) and choosing calm entrance verbs

Named recipes. No blueprint fits a push-in then pull-back mechanism demonstration (zoom-out-workspace-reveal forbids a zoom-in; camera-journey is a product-action shape), so the scene is composed from rules

camera.reason: The tile's own change carries the reveal. A camera move on top would give the eye two things to follow
camera.subject: the request rate limiter tile

objects.change: The request rate limiter tile, carried over from s09 while the other three limiter tiles recede, grows and turns into the surface of the central host. A bucket settles inside it.

moments.purpose: The bucket has to read as how the limiter the viewer already knows is built, not as a new fifth thing

recipes.purpose: Change the limiter tile into the host surface in one move so the viewer sees the bucket come from inside that limiter
Set the term 'token bucket' at display scale with strong weight contrast so it reads in the time it is on screen

moments.attention: the request rate limiter tile opening onto the bucket

narration.job: Name the algorithm and tie it to the limiter being opened
narration.guide: Under the hood, Stripe uses the token bucket algorithm.

moments.title: One bucket per user, on one host

camera.reason: The mechanism is per user, so the viewer should watch a single bucket closely enough to count its tokens
camera.subject: user A's bucket
camera.treatment: push in to one user's bucket

moments.purpose: Show that the bucket belongs to one user, which is what makes this the per-user cap, and that all the buckets share one host

recipes.purpose: Buckets arrive on the host as a short staggered group with little overshoot, calm explainer register
Push the world camera in on one user's bucket; the same world wrapper later pulls back in m6
Dim and soften the other users' buckets so the focal bucket owns the frame without removing them from the world

narration.job: Establish per-user ownership and the shared host before the mechanism runs
narration.guide: Every user has a bucket on a central host;

presenter.reason: Depends on the scene's delivery choice

moments.observation: A row of users on the left, each joined to its own bucket on a shared host plate. Then the view closes in on one user's bucket while the rest dim

audio.cue: A soft, even tick on each drip (suggestion)
audio.reason: Gives the drip a steady beat the ear can compare with the request rhythm

moments.title: Spend a token, drip one back

camera.reason: The viewer should compare two rates. A moving frame would blur that comparison
camera.subject: user A's bucket, its lane and the tap

objects.change: Requests travel from user A along a lane into the bucket mouth, each leaves with a token and continues to the API. A tap above the bucket releases one token per tick. The level holds at five

moments.purpose: Before state. The viewer needs the balance between spend and refill before seeing it break

recipes.purpose: Draw the request lane from the user through the bucket to the API before the first request uses it
Move requests along the drawn lane so each one visibly stops at the bucket, takes a token, and continues

A tap releases one token per tick into the bucket on a baked, deterministic schedule, and each spent token lifts out with its request. Nothing in the indexes covers a discrete fill-and-drain of countable tokens

moments.attention: the token level staying constant as tokens leave and arrive

narration.job: Describe the two flows, the spend and the refill
narration.guide: each request takes a token, and tokens drip back in at a steady rate.

presenter.reason: Depends on the scene's delivery choice

moments.observation: Each passing request takes one token out. A token drips in at a steady tick. Because the two rates match, the level stays where it is

audio.cue: The drip tick keeps its tempo under the burst (suggestion)
audio.reason: Makes it audible that the refill did not speed up

moments.title: Faster than the drip

camera.reason: Keep the same framing as m3 so the only difference the viewer sees is the request rate
camera.subject: user A's bucket

objects.change: Eight requests arrive within two ticks. The bucket goes from five tokens to zero while only two tokens drip in

moments.purpose: Action. The viewer should see that the rejection comes from the rates, with demand outpacing refill

recipes.purpose: The same lane motion as m3 at a tighter spacing, so the burst reads as more requests rather than faster ones
A slim level gauge on the bucket's side steps down with each spent token, so the drain can be read as a quantity

moments.attention: the falling token level against the unchanged drip

narration.job: State the cause of running dry
narration.guide: When requests arrive faster than the drip, the bucket runs dry.

presenter.reason: Depends on the scene's delivery choice

moments.observation: A burst of requests arrives close together. Tokens leave much faster than the tap refills them, the drip keeps its same slow tick, and the level falls to zero

audio.cue: A muted stop on the rejection, then the drip tick resumes (suggestion)
audio.reason: Marks the refusal without alarm and brings back the steady rate

moments.title: Empty means rejected

camera.reason: The consequence happens exactly where the mechanism played. Keep the viewer there
camera.subject: user A's bucket mouth

objects.change: Request 9 stops at the empty bucket mouth, is marked rejected and returns along the lane. The next drip adds one token, and the following request spends it and passes

moments.purpose: After state. The rejection is the consequence the viewer has just watched build up

recipes.purpose: The rejected request halts at the bucket mouth, takes the rejected mark, and travels back along its own lane. No catalogued rule covers a request turned back at a gate
The same tap as m3 adds one token after the rejection, showing that the drip alone brings capacity back

moments.attention: the rejected request at the empty bucket

narration.guide: When the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

presenter.reason: Depends on the scene's delivery choice

moments.observation: The next request reaches an empty bucket, finds no token, and is turned back to the user. Then one token drips in and a single paced request passes again

coverage.need: Show before, action and after: a bucket with tokens, requests consuming them faster than the drip, the empty bucket rejecting
Make the refill perceptible as steady and slower than a burst of requests
Connect the bucket back to the request rate limiter's per-user cap

delivery.note: Suggest generated-only or a hidden presenter for the mechanism (m2–m5). A recorded take could share the frame in m1 and m6.

content.question: How is a rate limiter actually built?
content.takeaway: Each user's bucket loses a token per request and refills at a steady drip; when requests outpace the drip the bucket empties and the next request is rejected. The buckets live in Redis.

continuity.exit: The Redis host held wide with one bucket per user, user A's bucket refilling from empty, and both operating options labelled. This is ready for s11, whose first concern is Redis or the limiter code failing
continuity.entry: From s09: the four limiter tiles as that scene left them, with the request rate limiter marked as the one that fires most. Only the request rate limiter tile carries forward into m1

treatments.text: Few words on screen, all short: the term 'token bucket', the label 'one bucket per user', the two flow labels, the token count readout, 'rejected', and 'Redis' with its two options. Narration never becomes paragraphs. Every invented value carries an 'illustrative' marker. Infrastructure names use a mono register. Content stays in the top ~83% of the frame.
treatments.camera: One world camera with exactly two moves: push in to user A's bucket in m2, pull back to the full host in m6. It holds for m1 and m3–m5 so the rates are compared in a still frame. Object-local motion (tokens, requests, tap, gauge) is written by its own recipes and never by the camera.
treatments.presenter: Delivery is undecided. Suggestion: generated-only or a presenter hidden for m2–m5, because the before, action and after need the viewer's full attention on one bucket. If a take exists, a shared framing could open m1 and return in m6. That is a note only, not a decision.

unresolved: Presenter visibility depends on the delivery choice
The source does not relate the drip rate to the request rate limiter's N, so the plan links them through identity (the bucket inside that limiter) and does not claim a numeric equality
The source does not say the burst allowance comes from bucket capacity, so the full bucket is never labelled as the burst allowance
The source does not name a response code for the empty-bucket rejection, so the plan shows 'rejected' without 429 or 503; s11 owns the status codes
Every token count, drip rate and burst size is illustrative; durations are estimates until audio exists
content.development: Open the request rate limiter, the identity the viewer already knows from the map, and find a token bucket inside it. Show the central host with one bucket per user, then push in on one user's bucket and run the mechanism in three states. Before: requests arrive at about the drip rate, so the level stays put. Action: a burst arrives faster than the drip and the level drains. After: the bucket is empty, the next request is turned back, and the drip carries on, which is what brings the bucket back. Pull back out to the whole host and name it: Redis, self-run or managed. The scene is one continuous world. The camera moves twice, in and back out, and holds still while the mechanism plays, so the viewer's eye stays on the rates.

demonstration.text: One user's bucket holds five tokens. The drip adds one token per tick. At first requests arrive about one per tick and the level holds. Then eight requests arrive within two ticks, the bucket drains to zero, and the ninth request is rejected. The next drip puts one token back.
